analysis.one_liner: Phases out the below-minimum wage for workers with disabilities and pays employers to shift them into regular jobs.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on July 24, 2025 with four original sponsors split evenly by party and referred to the Senate labor committee, which has taken no further action on it.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law currently lets some employers get a certificate to pay workers with disabilities less than the minimum wage. This bill would raise those wages step by step to the full minimum over five years, ban new certificates, and then end the program entirely. To soften the blow, it would pay states up to $15 million and individual employers up to $750,000 to reorganize so their workers hold regular community jobs at normal pay instead of segregated workshop jobs.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers with disabilities who are currently paid under these special certificates. Their wages would climb — to 60% of the federal minimum starting 90 days after enactment, then 70%, 80%, 90%, and the full minimum by year five — and states and employers would get grant money to help them move into regular jobs alongside non-disabled coworkers. The bill also requires an audit of at least 10% of certificate-holding employers and annual wage reports, so for the first time the practice would be systematically examined.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers with disabilities earning subminimum wages

how_it_helps.text: The bill raises the wage floor for certificate-holding employers in five annual steps, from 60% of the federal minimum wage to the full minimum wage by the fifth year after enactment.
It bars the Labor Department from issuing any new special certificates and makes every existing certificate legally worthless five years after enactment.

States that commit to transforming every certificate-holding employer in their borders can get grants of $3 million to $15 million over five years, and individual employers not covered by a state grant can get $200,000 to $750,000 over three years to convert to competitive integrated employment models.

The Labor Department must audit at least 10% of certificate-holding employers within a year, examining their wages and whether they help workers transition, and must report annually to Congress on how many workers are paid below the minimum and what happens to them.
The bill authorizes $200 million a year for fiscal years 2026 through 2030, with 1% set aside for a nonprofit technical assistance center.

analysis.who_pays: Employers holding special certificates, most of them nonprofit disability service providers whose staffing model depends on paying subminimum wages, would see their labor costs rise and their business model end within five years. Taxpayers would fund the grant programs if Congress appropriates the authorized $200 million a year.

drawbacks.text: Certificate-holder grants are capped at $750,000 over three years, and it is an open question whether that is enough for large operations built around subminimum-wage contracts to convert.
Workers with the most significant disabilities may find fewer workshop slots even though the bill requires them to be first in line for employment supports and integrated services.
The $200 million a year is authorized, not guaranteed; every year of funding would have to survive the appropriations process.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the workers covered, the bill is close to a pure gain: pay rises to the legal minimum and help arrives to find regular jobs. The real risk falls on the same group — if conversions are underfunded or community jobs do not materialize, some workers could lose the only employment setting available to them, and the bill's own evaluation and reporting machinery would not reveal that until late in the transition. Whether the bill works therefore depends heavily on Congress actually appropriating the grant money, which is not automatic.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on July 24, 2025, read twice, and sent to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where it has sat without a hearing, a markup, or a vote.

narrative.text: Senator Van Hollen introduced the bill jointly with Senators Daines, Gillibrand, and Blackburn, a mix of two Democrats and two Republicans.
Seven additional cosponsors joined, four Republicans and three Democrats, bringing the total to eleven.
The bill was referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on the day it was introduced, and the action history shows no further steps.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has had to change anything. Employers holding special certificates can keep paying below-minimum wages while the bill waits in committee.

sides.party_line_note: The record shows no opposition — the obstacle so far is committee inaction, not a voted no — and support is genuinely bipartisan, with the four original introducers split two Democrats and two Republicans and the seven later cosponsors split four Republicans and three Democrats.

industries.industry: Sheltered workshops and disability service providers holding 14(c) certificates
industries.note: These employers lose the legal ability to pay workers with disabilities less than the minimum wage within five years, which raises their labor costs. But they are also the beneficiaries of the bill's grant programs — up to $750,000 per employer, or up to $15 million per state — to fund their conversion to integrated employment, so the bill pays the very industry it is retiring.

industries.industry: Businesses that pay full minimum wage and compete with certificate holders
industries.note: Today a certified employer can underbid them by paying workers with disabilities less than the minimum wage for the same work. Ending the certificates removes that cost advantage.

industries.industry: Integrated employment and community support services sector
industries.note: The bill directs grant money toward integrated services, wraparound supports, and a nonprofit technical assistance center, creating funded demand for providers who help people with disabilities find and keep regular jobs.

analysis.trajectory: Bills that are only introduced and referred to committee rarely reach a vote — the committee must schedule a hearing or markup, and floor time must be found, before anything happens. With bipartisan sponsorship of eleven senators, the bill's best realistic paths are attachment to a larger workforce or disability bill, but on its own record it is likely to sit in committee unless the panel acts this Congress.
